'''''Draba verna''''' ([[syn.]] ''Erophila verna''), '''common whitlowgrass''', is a species of plant in the [[Brassicaceae|cabbage family]]. It is a small spring-flowering annual which is widely dispersed around the world, and which is found on walls, pavements and patches of bare ground. It has a complex taxonomy which is not yet fully elucidated.

==Description==
Common whitlowgrass is a spring-flowering annual, typically up to {{convert|10|cm|in|abbr=on|0}} tall (sometimes as much as {{convert|25|cm|in|abbr=on|0}}) with a basal rosette and one or more leafless flowering stems. It is variably hairy, sometimes almost completely glabrous (hairless), especially on the stems. The elliptical leaves are up to {{convert|20|mm|in|abbr=on|0}} long (exceptionally up to {{convert|35|mm|in|abbr=on|1}}) and {{convert|8|mm|in|abbr=on|1}} wide and are often entire, but sometimes with a single tooth on one or both sides, and they taper gradually into a more-or-less distinct petiole. The surfaces and margins usually have a scattering of hairs that are forked, or Y-shaped, at the tips. The central vein is faintly visible on the top side of the leaf but easily distinguishable on the underside. Mature leaves can turn a reddish colour.<ref name=rich>{{cite book| last = Rich| first = T.C.G.| year = 1991| title = Crucifers of Great Britain and Ireland | place = London| publisher = Botanical Society of the British Isles| isbn = 0901158208}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Sutton |first1=David |title=Field Guide to Wildflowers of Britain and Northern Europe |date=1988 |publisher=Kingfisher Books |isbn=1-85813-215-0}}</ref>
[[File:Draba verna flower.jpg|thumb|Flowers of common whitlowgrass]]
[[File:Draba verna leaves.jpg|thumb|The leaves are often covered with forked hairs]]

Flowering occurs in early spring, March–May in northern latitudes. Each stem (of which there can be several) bears a lax [[raceme]] of about 10 long-stalked flowers with 4 white petals, about {{convert|3|mm|in|abbr=on|1}} long, which are so deeply divided (bifid) that it can appear that there are 8 petals. The flowers have 6 stamens with yellow anthers, and one style. The sepals are about {{convert|2|mm|in|abbr=on|1}} long, green, hairy and often have a purplish margin. The fruit (called a silique), forms immediately after flowering while the petals are still present, due to self-pollination. It is oval to elliptical, flattened and up to {{convert|9|mm|in|abbr=on|1}} long by {{convert|3|mm|in|abbr=on|1}} wide with a persistent style at the tip Each silique contains a dozen or so round seeds in two "valves", which split open to leave just the transparent membrane between them, which looks like a tiny version of an [[Lunaria annua|honesty]] seedpod.<ref name=Rose>{{cite book |last1=Rose |first1=Francis |title=The Wild Flower Key |date=2006 |publisher=Frederick Warne |location=London|isbn=978-0-7232-5175-0}}</ref><ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref><ref name="rich" />
[[File:DrabaV4.jpg|thumb|The seedpods split open to leave just the translucent membrane that separates the valves.]]

In the summer months the seeds remain dormant, and they need about 3 months to after-ripen before they can germinate successfully,<ref name="Germinate">{{cite journal |last1=Baskin |first1=J.M. |last2=Baskin |first2=C.C.|year=1970 | title=Germination eco-physiology of Draba verna |journal=Bulletin of the Torrey Botanical Club| volume=97 | issue=1 | page=209| ref=JSTOR | doi=10.2307/2483459|jstor=2483459 }}</ref> during which time they need 5–7 weeks of sunlight or they will not germinate well in the autumn.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baskin |first1=J.M. |last2=Baskin |first2=C.C. |year=1972 | title=The Light Factor in the Germination Ecology of Draba verna | journal=American Journal of Botany| volume=57 | issue=7 | pages=756| ref=JSTOR | doi=10.2307/2441148|jstor=2441148 }}</ref> In experiments, they were found to germinate most successfully at 50% to 60% relative humidity.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baskin |first1=J.M. |last2=Baskin |first2=C.C.|year=1979 | title=Effect of Relative Humidity on Afterripening and Viability in Seeds of the Winter Annual Draba verna | journal=Botanical Gazette| volume=140 | issue=3 | pages=284–287| ref=JSTOR | doi=10.1086/337087|s2cid=85002496 }}</ref>
[[File:Erophila verna plant (12).jpg|thumb|Some leaves have a single tooth on one side of the leaf blade, resembling a whitlow.]]

==Taxonomy==
The taxonomy of the genus ''Draba'' is extraordinarily complex, particularly for ''Draba verna'', which is sometimes treated as a whole genus (''Erophila'' <small>DC</small>.) in its own right, with a number of different species and varieties listed under various treatments. The reason for this is that ''D. verna'' reproduces almost entirely by inbreeding (the flowers pollinating themselves immediately on opening), so a large number of genetically similar lines can be recognised. These lines can even have different chromosome numbers (or ploidy levels), making them less compatible with other plants even when cross-pollination does occur. A full list of synonyms, subspecies and varieties is given in the [https://www.gbif.org/dataset/b6349cdd-9d7e-4b23-8c05-a231f0ffa1a0 Brassicaceae Species Checklist]. The account here is for ''Draba verna'' <small>L.</small> in its original, aggregate, sense, although ''[[Draba praecox|D. praecox]]'' and ''[[Draba majuscula|D. majuscula]]'' can be viewed as separate species.<ref name="Thaden">{{cite journal |last1=Jordan-Thaden |first1=I. |last2=Hase |first2=I |last3=Al-Shehbaz |first3=I |last4=Koch |first4=M |year=2002 | title=Molecular data indicate complex intra- and intercontinental differentiation of American Draba (Brassicaceae) | journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden| volume=89 | issue=1 | pages=88–109| ref=JSTOR | doi=10.2307/3298659|jstor=3298659 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/part/16376 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jordan-Thaden |first1=I. E. |last2=Al-Shehbaz |first2=I.A. |last3=Koch |first3=M.A.|year=2013 | title=Species richness of the globally distributed, arctic–alpine genus Draba L. (Brassicaceae) | journal=Alpine Botany | volume=123 | issue=2 | pages=97–107| ref=JSTOR | doi=10.1007/s00035-013-0120-9|s2cid=16878175 }}</ref><ref name="rich" /><ref name="Stace" />

The chromosome number of ''Draba verna'' (as the segregate ''Erophila verna'' <small>(L.) DC.</small>) is 2n = 30-46. If it is treated as the aggregate, then ''D. majuscula'' has 2n = 14, and ''D. praecox'' has 2n = 48-56.<ref name="Stace" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jordan-Thaden |first1=I. |last2=Koch |first2=M.A.|year=2008 | title=Species richness and polyploid patterns in the genus ''Draba'' (Brassicaceae): a first global perspective | journal=Plant Ecology & Diversity | volume=1 | issue=2 | pages=255–263| ref=JSTOR | doi=10.1080/17550870802349112|s2cid=83865900 }}</ref>

The common name "whitlowgrass" refers to an old meaning of the word, which [[Aulus Cornelius Celsus]] described as "a small piece of flesh [which] sometimes grows out from the nail, causing great pain; the Greeks call it pterygium."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Celsus |first1=Aurus Cornelius |title=De Medicina |date= |url=https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Celsus/6*.html |access-date=22 March 2023}}</ref>
The leaves of whitlowgrass sometimes have a single forward-pointing tooth on one side, thus resembling this condition. The "grass" part of the name simply means "plant" and does not imply that it is in the botanical [[Poaceae|grasses family]]. Other common names for it include "spring draba", "shadflower", "nailwort", "vernal whitlow grass" and "early whitlow grass".

==Identification==
The combination of bifid petals (sometimes giving the impression of having flowers with 8 petals) and leafless stems makes this species very easy to identify. Separating it from the critical segregates ''D. majuscula'' and ''D. praecox'', if you choose to accept them, is much more difficult. The depth of division of the petals, the hairiness of the leaves and stems, and the length of the petiole are all useful field characters.<ref name="rich" /><ref>{{cite book |last1=Rich |first1=T.C.G. |last2=Jermy |first2=A.C. |title=Plant Crib 1998 |date=1998 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London |isbn=0-901-158-28-3}}</ref>
[[File:Draba verna whole.jpg|thumb|Whitlowgrasses can look as if they have 8 petals]]

==Distribution and status==
Common whitlowgrass is native to Europe, western Asia and parts of North Africa southwards to Ethiopia.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jonsell |first1=B.|year=2000 | title=A new subspecific combination in Erophila (Brassicaceae) from Ethiopia | journal=Nordic Journal of Botany| volume=20 | issue=2 | pages=201| ref=JSTOR | doi=10.1111/j.1756-1051.2000.tb01569.x| doi-access=free }}</ref> It is also widely established in the temperate regions of the Americas, Australia, New Zealand and Japan.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Global Biodiversity Information Facility |title=Draba verna L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/7473187 |access-date=19 March 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Plants of the World Online |title=Draba verna L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:283173-1 |access-date=19 March 2023}}</ref> It has been postulated that it was brought to North America when the European colonizers came to the New World.<ref name="Colonizers">{{cite journal |last1=Ugarte |first1=E. |last2=Lira |first2=F.|last3=Fuentes |first3=N |last4=Klotz |first4=S |year=2011 | title=Vascular alien flora, Chile | journal= Check List| volume=7 | issue=3 | pages=365| ref=JSTOR | doi=10.15560/7.3.365|doi-access=free }}</ref>
[[File:Draba verna sward.jpg|thumb|Whitlowgrass grows on bare soils, with the minimum of competition]]

It is sometimes listed as an invasive species in places where it is introduced, such as the United States, but there is no suggestion that it causes any harm.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States |title=Spring whitlowgrass, Draba verna |url=https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.html?sub=5557 |access-date=19 March 2023}}</ref> Its global status has not been assessed,<ref>{{cite web |last1=European Environment Agency |title=Erophila verna subsp. verna |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/162790 |access-date=19 March 2023}}</ref> but in countries where it is native it is generally listed as "Least Concern."<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cheffings |first1=C.M. | last2=Farrell |first2=L. |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain |date=2005 |publisher=Joint Nature Conservation Committee |location=Peterborough}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Inventaire National du Patrimoine Naturel |title=Draba verna L. |url=https://inpn.mnhn.fr/espece/cd_nom/95372/tab/statut |access-date=20 March 2023}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
Typical places for common whitlowgrass to grow include almost any place where there is bare soil, including limestone pavements, sand dunes, field margins, urban pavements and quarry waste.<ref name=Atlas>{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=C.D. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |last3=Dines |first3=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford}}</ref>

Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 3, F = 3, R = 6, N = 3, and S = 0,<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf|accessdate=29 May 2017}}</ref> which shows that it favours relatively dry, neutral soils and low levels of fertility.

The UK's database of [http://dbif.brc.ac.uk/hostsresults.aspx?hostid=2110 Insects and their Food Plants] lists just 4 species that feed on common whitlowgrass. Three of these are weevils: the cabbage leaf weevil, ''Ceutorhynchus contractus'',  the cabbage stem weevil, ''C. quadridens'', and ''C. hirtulus''. The other is a butterfly, the [[Anthocharis cardamines|orange tip]], which is a common species whose larvae feed on the flowers of plants in the cabbage family.

Two species of downy mildew infect common whitlowgrass, particularly when it is suffering from water stress: ''[[Hyaloperonospora]] erophilae'' coats the leaves and turns them chlorotic, whereas ''H. praecox'' has more localised and less obvious symptoms. They can be identified by the differences in their [[Haustorium|haustoria]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Voglmayr |first1=Hermann |last2=Göker |first2=Markus |title=Morphology and phylogeny of Hyaloperonospora erophilae and H. praecox sp. nov., two downy mildew species co-occurring on Draba verna sensu lato |journal=Mycol. Progress |date=2011 |volume=10 |issue=3 |pages=283–292 |doi=10.1007/s11557-010-0699-9|s2cid=31301203 }}</ref>

==Uses==
There appear to be no recorded uses for whitlowgrass.<ref name=Allen>{{cite book |last1=Allen |first1=D.E. |last2=Hatfield |first2=Gabrielle |title=Medicinal plants in folk tradition: an ethnobotany of Britain and Ireland |date=2004 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, Oregon |isbn=0-88192-638-8 |url=https://www.agrifs.ir/sites/default/files/Medicinal%20Plants%20in%20Folk%20Tradition%20%7BDavid%20E.%20Allen%7D%20%5B0881926388%5D%20%28Timber%20Press%2C%20Inc%20-%202004%29.pdf}}</ref> In the 1600s [[Nicholas Culpeper|Culpeper]] described it as "exceedingly good for those imposthumes in the joints, and under the nails, which they call Whitlows, Felons, Andicorns and Nail-wheals",<ref>{{cite book |last1=Culpeper |first1=Nicholas |title=The Complete Herbal |date=1850 |publisher=Thomas Kelly |location=London |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513}}</ref> but Vickery<ref>{{cite book |last1=Vickery |first1=Roy |title=Vickery's Folk Flora |date=2019 |publisher=Weidenfeld & Nicolson |location=London |isbn=978-1-4746-0462-8}}</ref> explains that it was never really used in folk medicine either in Britain or Ireland. Neither is it mentioned in American herbals.<ref name=Grieve>{{cite book |last1=Grieve |first1=Maud |title=A Modern Herbal |date=1931 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0-486-22798-7}}</ref> Presumably Culpeper ascribed to it this property according to the [[doctrine of signatures]], owing to the unusual shape of the leaves.
